analysis.one_liner: Guarantees health coverage for every American through regulated private health plans with capped premiums.
analysis.headline: President Clinton's universal health care bill cleared a Senate committee and was placed on the Senate calendar in July 1994, but the Senate never voted on it before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the Senate companion to President Clinton's Health Security Act. It would have required every eligible American to enroll in a certified health plan, guaranteed a comprehensive benefit package with out-of-pocket costs capped at $2,500 per person per year, banned insurers from denying coverage for pre-existing conditions, and capped how fast premiums could grow. It died without ever coming to a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Every American, especially the roughly 37-40 million uninsured and anyone with a pre-existing condition who could be priced out or denied coverage. Workers would keep coverage when changing jobs; families would face a hard cap of $2,500 individual / $3,000 family in annual out-of-pocket costs; low-income families would get reduced cost sharing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with pre-existing conditions

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every eligible individual to a comprehensive benefit package covering hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health, dental, vision, and preventive services, with a health security card [S2][S3].
Prohibits health plans from discriminating based on medical history, pre-existing conditions, or genetic predisposition, and requires open enrollment with no waiting periods [S2][S3].
Caps annual out-of-pocket expenses at $2,500 for an individual and $3,000 for a family, with cost-sharing reductions for low-income families [S2][S3].
Limits how fast community-rated premiums can grow through National Health Board premium caps, and requires employers to cover at least 80% of the premium for many employees [S2][S3].
Allows any state, with federal approval, to adopt a single-payer system, and preserves Medicare for Medicare-eligible people [S2][S3].
Adds long-term care benefits, including a voluntary long-term care insurance program for people 35 and over covering nursing home stays [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially small businesses, would owe premium contributions of at least 80% of the cost for many employees. Taxpayers would fund capped federal payments to states, expanded public health programs, and long-term care. Younger and healthier people would pay community-rated premiums that no longer reflect their lower risk. Health insurers would lose the ability to underwrite, deny, or price coverage based on health status.

drawbacks.text: The bill's funding mechanism was left unresolved: the committee only stated its 'sense' that financing sources outside its jurisdiction should be added when the bill was enacted, leaving the question of who pays new taxes open [S2][S3].
The committee filed minority views against the measure, and it attracted zero Senate cosponsors [S4][S5].

Premium caps and federal premium targets give a new National Health Board broad power over health plan revenues, which insurers argued would force plans out of business and lead to limits on care; critics also noted the bill's employer mandate would cost small businesses [S2].

The plan kept coverage running through private health plans and employer channels rather than a government program, making the system complex to administer; even supporters acknowledged the regional premium-targeting and risk-adjustment machinery was untested [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have ended the largest gaps in American health security — uninsurance, coverage loss when changing jobs, and denial for pre-existing conditions — while imposing real costs: new employer mandates, unresolved financing, and a powerful new federal board capping premiums. Its design kept private insurers as the delivery channel, which preserved industry choice but limited how much costs could be squeezed. The unresolved funding question was a genuine weakness, but the bill at least moved the issue to the floor of the debate rather than dying quietly.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee reported it as an original bill and it was placed on the Senate calendar, but it never came to the floor, and the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee ordered and reported the measure as an original bill on June 9 and July 19, 1994, with written report 103-317 and minority views filed [S5].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 525 on July 19, 1994 [S5][S3].
No further action was taken; no vote ever occurred in the Senate, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health insurance industry and other opponents of restructuring the health system benefited: the existing employer-based, individually underwritten insurance system continued unchanged, and the roughly 37-40 million uninsured remained without guaranteed coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of health system restructuring; the uninsured stayed uninsured

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MA), sponsor and chair of the Labor and Human Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and reported it to the Senate from his committee as an original measure, placing it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Made the Health Security Act his signature legislative initiative and pressed Congress to pass it in 1994.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Minority party, 44 of 100 Senate seats at the time
against.what_they_did: Uniformly opposed the Health Security Act and made clear it could not reach the 60 votes needed to end debate, so leadership never brought it to the floor.

against.name: Health insurance industry (Health Insurance Association of America)
against.role: Industry trade group for health insurers
against.what_they_did: Funded a nationwide advertising campaign ('Harry and Louise') arguing the plan would limit choice and drive up costs, helping turn public opinion against the bill.

against.name: Small business groups (National Federation of Independent Business)
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the employer mandate requiring businesses to pay most workers' premiums.

against.name: George J. Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Announced in August 1994 that the Senate would not take up the health care bill because supporters could not muster the votes to break a filibuster.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Democratic measure sponsored by Senator Kennedy with zero Republican cosponsors and filed minority views; Republicans opposed it nearly uniformly, while some conservative Democrats also balked, leaving the Democratic leadership without the votes to hold a floor debate.

industries.note: The bill stripped insurers of the power to deny or price coverage by health status, imposed premium caps and community rating, and would have forced many small insurers out — but every American would be required to buy coverage through certified health plans, guaranteeing them a captive customer base. The industry fought the bill because the regulations threatened far more revenue than guaranteed enrollment promised.

Universal coverage would end most uncompensated care and guarantee payment, but premium caps and federal payment limits would squeeze hospital revenues. Safety-net hospitals with low-income patients would receive specified payments [S2].

Outpatient prescription drugs would become a covered benefit for tens of millions of newly insured people, a large new market, but premium caps and a federal price-and-spending monitoring program would pressure drug prices [S2][S3].

Qualifying employers would have to cover at least 80% of employees' premiums and meet new recordkeeping and retiree obligations, though employers would also benefit from capped premium growth [S2][S3].
